response.answer: For paired studies, a sample size of approximately 40 pairs is needed to detect a 0.05 Dice improvement with SD=0.10 at 80-90% power and alpha=0.05. This assumes a correlation of 0.5 between measures.

results.title: Sample size calculation for paired samples t-test with correlation: How to simulate power? - Cross Validated
results.content: # Sample size calculation for paired samples t-test with correlation: How to simulate power? I am calculating the sample size for a paired samples t-test with a correlation between samples of 0.05. pwrss.t.2means(mu1 = 1.5, mu2 = 0.5, sd1 = 1.4, sd2 = 1.1, paired = TRUE, paired.r = 0.50, power = .80, alpha = 0.05, alternative = "not equal") Difference between Two means (Paired Samples t Test) H0: mu1 = mu2 HA: mu1 != mu2 ------------------------------ Statistical power = 0.8 n = 15 ------------------------------ Alternative = “not equal” Degrees of freedom = 14 Non-centrality parameter = 3.034 Type I error rate = 0.05 Type II error rate = 0.2. * $\begingroup$ /questions/15011 gives general-purpose methods to create variables with any desired correlation--and it's not limited to specific distributions (like Normal distributions). First, note that the t-test for paired data is actually a one-sample t-test on the *differences* between the pairs. Assuming a bivariate normal distribution, the distribution of the differences is also normal with mean $\mu\_2 - \mu\_1$ and standard deviation $\sqrt{\sigma\_1^2 + \sigma\_2^2 -2\rho\sigma\_1\sigma\_2}$, where $\rho$ is the correlation between the pairs. library(MASS) n_pairs <- 15 # Number of pairs mu_diff <- 0.5-1.5 # Difference in means sd_vec <- c(1.4, 1.1) # Standard deviations rho <- 0.5 # Correlation sd_diff <- sqrt(sum(sd_vec^2) - 2*rho*prod(sd_vec)) # Standard deviation of the difference # Run simulations set.seed(1234) res <- replicate(1e5, { x <- rnorm(n_pairs, mu_diff, sd_diff) # Sample from normal distribution for the differences t.test(x, mu = 0)$p.value # Run the t test, save p-value }) # Simulated power mean(res <= 0.05) [1] 0.80331. answered Feb 24, 2025 at 14:09. * $\begingroup$ @R-ista I changed the example to make it more simple: You only need to simulate one random variable, the differences. results.title: Power Analysis for Paired Sample t-test
results.content: # Power Analysis for Paired Sample t-test. One is to calculate the necessary sample size for a specified power. The other aspect is to calculate the power when given a specific sample size. The smaller the Type I error rate, the larger the sample size required for the same power. Likewise, the smaller the Type I error rate, the smaller the power for the same sample size. In SPSS, it is fairly straightforward to perform a power analysis for the paired sample t-test using SPSS’s **power means related** command. For the calculation of Example 1, we can set the power at different levels and calculate the sample size for each level. > power means related /parameters test=nondirectional significance=0.05 power=.8 sd=5 mean=5. > power means related /parameters test=nondirectional significance=0.05 power=.85 sd=5 mean=5. > power means related /parameters test=nondirectional significance=0.05 power=.9 sd=5 mean=5. What does this mean for our sample size calculation? > power means related /parameters test=nondirectional significance=0.01 power=.85 sd=5 mean=5. As you can see, the sample size goes up from 13 to 17 for specified power of .85 when alpha drops from .05 to .01. This means if we want our test to be more reliable, i.e., not rejecting the null hypothesis in case it is true, we will need a larger sample size. > power means related /parameters test=nondirectional power=.90 significance=.01 sd=5 mean=5. How much statistical power does her design have to detect the difference of 5 seconds with standard deviation of 10 seconds? > power means related /parameters test=nondirectional significance=0.05 npairs=35 sd=10 mean=0 5. Now, let’s recalculate the power for one-tailed paired-sample t-test. > power means related /parameters test=directional significance=0.05 npairs=35 sd=10 mean=0 5. You have probably noticed that the way to conduct the power analysis for paired-sample t-test is the same as for the one-sample t-test. This is due to the fact that in the paired-sample t-test we compute the difference in the two scores for each subject and then compute the mean and standard deviation of the differences. If the distribution is skewed, then a small sample size may not have the power shown in the results, because the value in the results is calculated using the method based on the normality assumption.

results.title: Power Analysis and Sample Size Calculation in Experimental Studies | by Maria Gusarova | Medium
results.content: ## Learn How Power Analysis and Sample Size Calculation Enhance the Reliability of Experimental Results. While the statistical significance calculation helps determine whether an experiment’s result is due to chance or a real effect, you may require additional steps. It helps to avoid errors by determining the sample size to ensure that your study has sufficient power to detect a true effect while still controlling the risk of falsely rejecting the null hypothesis. It involves considering four important factors: sample size, effect size, significance, and statistical power, which are related to each other. For example, a larger sample size generally increases the statistical power and the likelihood of detecting a true effect. While we don’t know the effect size since we didn’t run the experiment yet, let’s assume four different effect sizes and calculate the required minimum sample size for each to reach 80% of the power by using the above formula:. For example, to have 80% power in the 0.10% effect size, we require 615,000 customers to be in the experiment.
